The eigenvalue equation is
\[
A_y\phi=a\phi,\qquad 
A_y=\frac{h}{4\pi}
\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\ i&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Since
\[
S=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\ i&0\end{pmatrix}
\]
has characteristic equation
\[
\det(S-\lambda I)=\lambda^2-1=0,
\]
its eigenvalues are \(\lambda=\pm1\). Therefore, the eigenvalues of \(A_y\) are
\[
a_\pm=\pm\frac{h}{4\pi},
\]
which are real. The normalized eigenvectors are
\[
\phi_+=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\ i\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\phi_-=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\ -i\end{pmatrix}.
\]

An eigenfunction of \(A_y\) is also an eigenfunction of the total squared angular momentum \(A^2\), since for spin \(1/2\), \(A^2\) is proportional to the identity matrix. However, it is not an eigenfunction of \(A_z\), because \(A_y\) and \(A_z\) do not commute and have different eigenvectors.

Answer: C
